data.title: Linear and whorled nevoid hypermelanosis — viva
data.summary: Pigmentary disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Linear and whorled nevoid hypermelanosis** (Pigmentary disorders)_

**Q1. What is linear and whorled nevoid hypermelanosis (LWNH)?**
- Sporadic mosaic disorder of pigmentation with streaks and whorls of macular hyperpigmentation following Blaschko's lines, appearing at birth or in the first weeks of life; progresses in first 1–2 years then stabilises
- Mosaic chromosomal abnormalities (trisomy 7, 18, X-chromosome mosaicism) in some

**Q2. Clinical features.**
- Brown macules in linear streaks and whorls ('marble-cake' pattern) on trunk and limbs, sparing face, palms, soles, mucosa, eyes; no preceding inflammation, vesicles or verrucous stages
- Usually isolated, but may have associated anomalies (CNS — seizures, developmental delay; cardiac defects, skeletal asymmetry) — 'LWNH syndrome'

**Q3. Histopathology.**
- Increased basal layer melanin, prominent melanocytes; no pigment incontinence (differentiates from incontinentia pigmenti stage 3)

**Q4. Differential diagnosis.**
- Incontinentia pigmenti (X-linked dominant, girls; inflammatory vesicular → verrucous → hyperpigmented → atrophic stages; pigment incontinence; eye, teeth, CNS)
- Linear epidermal naevus (raised, verrucous), hypomelanosis of Ito (hypopigmented whorls — the 'negative' counterpart), Goltz syndrome (focal dermal hypoplasia), segmental pigmentation disorder, chimerism, X-linked reticulate pigmentary disorder

**Q5. Management.**
- Reassurance; screen for systemic anomalies (development, neurology, cardiac, skeletal); genetic consultation/karyotype of skin fibroblasts if systemic features
- No effective treatment; camouflage; lasers rarely help

**Q6. What are Blaschko's lines and why does LWNH follow them?**
- Lines of embryonic migration/proliferation of ectodermal cells — V on the back, S-shaped on the trunk sides, linear on limbs; a post-zygotic mutation in a melanocyte or keratinocyte clone becomes visible along these lines (cutaneous mosaicism)

**Q7. Name other disorders following Blaschko's lines.**
- Incontinentia pigmenti, hypomelanosis of Ito, epidermal naevus/ILVEN, nevus sebaceous, lichen striatus, linear LP, linear porokeratosis, Goltz syndrome, CHILD syndrome, X-linked dominant chondrodysplasia punctata (Conradi–Hünermann), segmental Darier's disease, blaschkitis

**Q8. What investigations are needed when LWNH has extracutaneous features?**
- Neurological assessment, EEG if seizures, MRI brain; echocardiography; skeletal survey for asymmetry; ophthalmology; karyotype on cultured skin fibroblasts (blood karyotype may be normal in mosaicism) — genetic counselling

**Q9. Does pigment fade?**
- Pigmentation is usually stable after early childhood, sometimes fades partially with age; no malignant potential

**Q10. Differentiate LWNH from incontinentia pigmenti in detail.**
- IP: X-linked dominant (IKBKG), girls; 4 stages (vesicular → verrucous → hyperpigmented → atrophic/ hypopigmented); eosinophilia; pigment incontinence; teeth, hair, nail, eye, CNS defects
- LWNH: sporadic, both sexes, no vesicles/ warty stage, no eosinophilia, basal hypermelanosis without incontinence

**Q11. What is hypomelanosis of Ito?**
- 'Negative' of LWNH — hypopigmented streaks/ whorls along Blaschko lines from birth/ early infancy; chromosomal mosaicism; associated CNS (seizures, intellectual disability), musculoskeletal and eye anomalies in ~30–60% — needs evaluation

**Q12. What is segmental pigmentation disorder?**
- Block-like (checkerboard) hyper- or hypopigmented patch with sharp midline demarcation (not Blaschkoid) from birth, stable; benign, no systemic association

**Q13. Explain the concept of cutaneous mosaicism types (Happle).**
- Type 1 (Blaschko lines narrow/ broad bands), type 2 (checkerboard), type 3 (phylloid — leaf-like), type 4 (patchy without midline separation), type 5 (lateralisation — CHILD); segmental type 1 and 2 manifestations of autosomal dominant disorders (superimposed mosaicism)

**Q14. Can LWNH be familial or syndromic?**
- Mostly sporadic; rare familial cases and associations with chromosomal mosaicism (trisomy 7, 14, 18, 20, X), neurological, cardiac and skeletal anomalies; genetic testing on skin fibroblasts if systemic features

**Q15. How does Wood's lamp help in pigmentary disorders?**
- 365 nm UVA absorbed by epidermal melanin: epidermal hyperpigmentation is accentuated (melasma epidermal type, freckles, CALM), dermal pigment is not; depigmentation (vitiligo, piebaldism) shows bright chalk-white; hypopigmentation (nevus depigmentosus, PA, IGH) shows dull off-white; also fluorescence of infections (PV yellow, erythrasma coral-red)

## Quick spotter facts
- Swirls of brown pigment along Blaschko lines from infancy without preceding blisters — LWNH
- No pigment incontinence (vs IP)

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Mosaic pigmentary disorders). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
